data: Much of the appeal of William Shakespeare’s seemingly inexhaustible power as a playwright lies in some of the most astonishing adaptations of his plays. This course will discuss how his plays have travelled across culture and medium, regions and most importantly, languages; and how the inherent potency of a Shakespearean play is unlocked in tongues far removed from the original. By bringing together some of his most well- known plays to stand in comparison with some of the most interesting and landmark cinematic adaptations, the course hopes to highlight both older and newer issues that have surfaced in Shakespearean studies over the years: from honour, state, authority, ambition, filial love, jealousy and madness to the more recent explorations of race, culture, sexuality, identity, gender and authorship itself. Also, the course would want to understand the politics and poetics of adaptation, elemental film theory and f ilm form, the language of cinema and how iconic texts perform as visual imagery. The primary focus of the course are four of Shakespeare’s most canonical works: Macbeth, Hamlet, King Lear and Julius Caesar. Having said that, the course will immediately get into challenging the very idea of their canonicity by entering them into a productive encounter with their cinematic adaptations. These adaptations, some of which will be studied closely, not only reinterpret these much revered literary classics, but also tend to push them away from having an ontological centre. To that end, the course is equally a study of how literary texts are both iconised and destabilized by the image.
